claims.quote: (3) A direction that the defendant file with the court a written pleading in response to the complaint within 30 days after summons is served on the defendant.
claims.note: The quoted period starts when the summons is served.

claims.claim: Talking with the collector or their lawyer does not pause the deadline.
claims.note: The statute distinguishes a filed response from a conversation but does not say whether a conversation affects the deadline.

claims.claim: A promise of more time must be in writing before it can be relied on.
claims.note: No rule on the effect of an oral or written extension was provided.

claims.claim: A written promise also needs confirmation from the court clerk or a lawyer before it can be relied on.
claims.note: The statute mentions consulting an attorney, not a confirmation procedure involving either an attorney or a clerk.

claims.claim: The answer applies any time before a response is filed.
claims.quote: within 30 days after summons is served on the defendant.
claims.note: The absence of a filed response does not establish that the stated period has started or that it remains open.

flags.text: The cited statute establishes what the summons must say, not what pauses the deadline or makes an extension effective.
“Any time before a response is filed” includes time before service and after the stated deadline.
“Do not rely on a promise” gives the reader a specific reliance test that the source does not establish.
A reader could take a writing and informal confirmation as sufficient and delay filing. The statute warns of default upon the plaintiff’s application if the defendant does not respond.

result.summary: The source supports the 30-day period after service. It does not resolve the question about phone calls or support the draft’s test for relying on a promise of more time.
